title: Build a mixed pallet layer so each top carton sits level on two equal-height cartons
instruction: Stand the four blue and green cartons upright on the brown pallet, then lay each orange carton level across two of them that are the same height.
context: Workers who hand-build mixed pallets pair cases of equal height in a layer so the next layer sits flat; a case laid across a short and a tall carton rests on one edge, crushes the taller carton's corner and slides off when the truck brakes. Done by: hand laborers and freight, stock and material movers; warehouse order pickers.
setup: Positions are given from the arm bases: 'in front' is the distance forward from the line through both arm bases, 'left' or 'right' the distance from the midpoint between them (each arm base is 30.5 cm from it). A brown painted plywood board stands in for a pallet deck: 20 cm front to back, 18 cm side to side, 1.5 cm thick, fixed to the table (clamped or taped) with its centre on the midline 24 cm in front, so it covers 14 to 34 cm in front and 9 cm either side of the midline. Four plain, unmarked cardboard base cartons with a 6 x 6 cm footprint: two short blue ones (4 cm tall, 150 g) and two tall green ones (6 cm tall, 200 g). On the left, the blue one stands with its centre 15 cm in front and 38 cm left, the green one 25 cm in front and 38 cm left. On the right, the green one stands 15 cm in front and 30 cm right, the blue one 25 cm in front and 30 cm right. Two orange cardboard top cartons (13 cm long, 6 cm wide, 3 cm tall, 200 g) lie flat on the left with their long sides pointing away from the arms, centres 20 cm in front and 16.5 cm and 27 cm left. All cartons are square to the table edges; a tape outline on the table marks each carton's start. Nothing else is on the table. No carton has to pass from one arm to the other: each orange carton can be laid across the midline by the left arm.
scoring: A base carton counts when it stands flat on the deck (a blue one on either 6 x 6 cm face, its 4 cm edges within 5 degrees of vertical; a green cube, which has no up side, on any face, one set of its edges within 5 degrees of vertical), its bottom within 3 mm of the deck's top face (standing on the deck, not on another carton), its footprint entirely on the deck, and it is still: 0.03 each, 0.12 for all four. An orange carton earns 0.44 when it lies on either big (13 x 6 cm) face across two counted base cartons whose top faces are within 5 mm of the same height, resting on their top faces (its lowest point within 0.5 mm of them, so a carton held even 1 mm above them doesn't count; in a real trial the gripper must have let go of it), at least 40 mm of its length over each of the two, a gap of at most 20 mm between them (along its length), at most 15 mm of it past the outline of the two on any side, tilted at most 2 degrees and still; tilted more than 2 but at most 5 degrees, the same earns 0.22. An orange carton resting on one base carton, on the deck, on the other orange carton or anywhere else earns nothing. All four base cartons on the deck and both orange cartons level on equal pairs: 1.0. If any orange carton is down on a base carton standing on the deck (that base carton's footprint within the deck's outline; footprints overlapping by at least 10 mm each way, seen from above; and the orange carton's lowest point at most 1 cm above that carton's top face) and is tilted more than 5 degrees, the score is 0: that is a case across a short and a tall carton (about 11 degrees here) or on its edge. An orange carton still carried higher than that, at any tilt, or tipped onto a base carton that is off the deck (still on the table or knocked off), does not trigger this rule and earns nothing itself.
reset_notes: Take the cartons off the deck and stand each back in its tape outline: the blues and greens upright as listed, the orange cartons flat with their long sides pointing away from the arms. The deck stays fixed. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Approximate: each carton is one rigid box of uniform density, so cartons don't crush or bulge and a carton across unequal heights stays intact; its tilt stands in for the damage. The deck is a fixed board, not a slatted pallet. Every object, the deck included, has the same rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), grippier than cardboard on plywood. Transit forces (braking, vibration) are not simulated; level support on equal heights is scored instead.
